name: Amram (Moses' father)
title: Levite and ancestor of Israel's priestly and prophetic line
summary: Amram belonged to the Kohathite clan within the tribe of Levi and became the father of three of the most central figures in Israel's early history: Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. He married Jochebed, his father's sister, thereby laying the foundation for a family that would decisively shape Israel's religious and national identity. Through his son Aaron, the priestly service at the sanctuary was established, and through Moses, the Torah and the covenant between God and Israel were conveyed. Amram's life fell in a time when the Israelites lived under harsh slavery in Egypt, and his descendants became the instruments God used to liberate His people. His lifespan of 137 years places him among the last with the characteristically high longevity from the early biblical generations. The clan bearing his name—the Amramites—held a special position among the Levites with responsibility for the most holy objects of the tabernacle, including the ark of the covenant.

keyEvents.title: Amram's Lineage
keyEvents.description: Amram was the son of Kohath and grandson of Levi, thus belonging to the Levitical tribe that would later serve at the sanctuary.

keyEvents.title: Marriage to Jochebed
keyEvents.description: Amram married Jochebed, his father's sister, and together they had three children who would all play decisive roles in Israel's history. This type of marriage was later explicitly forbidden in the legislation given through Moses.

keyEvents.title: Amram's Lifespan
keyEvents.description: Amram lived 137 years, and his life spanned a significant period of Israel's stay in Egypt.

keyEvents.title: Service of the Amramites at the Tabernacle
keyEvents.description: Amram is mentioned as the ancestor of the Amramite clan, one of the Levitical families responsible for the tabernacle and its holy objects, including the ark of the covenant and the lampstand.

keyEvents.title: Amram in the Genealogies of Chronicles
keyEvents.description: The genealogies in Chronicles confirm Amram's role as father to Aaron and Moses, establishing the priestly line that passed through his descendants.

keyEvents.title: Amram's Descendants in the Census
keyEvents.description: In the census, Amram and Jochebed are named as parents of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam, confirming the family's central role in Israel's history.

versions.summary: Amram was a Levite from Kohath's clan and father to Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. He married Jochebed, his father's sister, and through his descendants both the priesthood and prophetic service in Israel were established. He lived during a time when the Israelites were oppressed in Egypt.
versions.title: The Faithful Father of the Levites
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Faithful Father of the Levites' is somewhat imprecise. Amram was not the father of the entire tribe of Levi, but rather the father of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. A more accurate title would be 'Levite and Father of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam'.; [major] Amram lived in the period before the Exodus from Egypt. He likely died before the actual exodus itself. The time designation 'Exodus' can be defended since his life is closely tied to this period, but his life primarily fell within the era of slavery in Egypt. Nevertheless, 'Exodus' is the closest available category for this period.; [minor] The dating 'c. 1600–1463 BC' is very specific and difficult to verify. The Bible states that he lived 137 years (Exod 6:20), but exact dates are debated. A more cautious formulation might be appropriate, though this is acceptable as an estimate.; [major] The role 'leader' is not documented in the Bible for Amram. There is no biblical text describing him as a leader. His primary roles were Levite and father (patriarch within a family context). 'Levite' should be added as a role.; [minor] The summary is good, but the phrasing 'his father's sister' should be clarified. In Exod 6:20 it states that Jochebed was his 'aunt' (father's sister), while in Num 26:59 she is described as 'Levi's daughter'. Regardless, the current wording is acceptable based on Exod 6:20.; [minor] In the event 'Amram's Place in the Genealogy', reference is made to Num 3:19,27. Verse 19 mentions Kohath's sons (including Amram), but verse 27 concerns the clan of the Amramites. The reference is correct, but verses 19 and 27 are not contiguous—it could have been clearer to separate them or include the intervening verses.; [minor] The event 'Amram in First Chronicles' refers to bookId 13 (1 Chr), chapter 6, verses 2–3. In the Hebrew numbering these verses may vary, but the reference to 1 Chr 6:2–3 is standard and correct.; [minor] It could have been useful to include a reference to Num 26:58–59, which mentions Amram and Jochebed's marriage and their children, providing further details about the family line.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a profile like Amram, there are several interesting linguistic, theological, and historical details that should be covered.

versions.title: Levite and father of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam
versions.reason: [major] Amram lived in Egypt before the Exodus period. He died before the Exodus took place. His time belongs to the period in Egypt that is best classified under 'patriarchs' or possibly the transition to 'exodus', but 'exodus' refers primarily to the actual departure events and the wilderness journey. However, one could argue that his life falls just prior to the exodus era. Given that his children were part of the Exodus generation, 'exodus' is acceptable though borderline.; [minor] Since this is version 2 and the previous version had a similar opening ('Amram was a Levite from the family of Kohath and father of Moses, Aaron and Miriam. He married Jochebed, s...'), the text should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish it from version 1. The summary should have a different angle and structure.; [minor] 'Patriarch' may be somewhat misleading for Amram – the term is usually used of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. 'Ancestor' or 'family head' would have been more precise. In addition, the role 'ancestor of the Amramites' could have been mentioned.; [minor] Some translations and Hebrew texts spell 'Jishar' as 'Jishar' or 'Kishar'. It is worth verifying that the id 'jishar' is consistent with the rest of the database.; [minor] Verses 19 and 27 in Numbers 3 are not entirely coherent – verse 19 mentions Kohath's sons, while verse 27 mentions the Amramites. Consider whether verses 27–31 would have provided better coverage of the responsibilities of the Amramites.; [minor] 1 Chronicles 6:2–3 is a correct reference, but bookId 13 corresponds to 1 Chronicles only in certain numbering systems. In the standard Protestant order, 1 Chronicles is bookId 13. This appears correct.; [minor] The footnote's wording 'the marriage laws in the books of Moses were codified after the patriarchal period' could be perceived as a theologically controversial claim. It would be better to phrase it more neutrally, for example that the laws were given to Moses after such marriages had occurred in earlier generations.

versions.reason: [minor] The reference to 'Numbers' is an unnecessarily explicit book name in the description. It is cleaner to use a more neutral formulation such as 'In the census of the Levites...' or similar.; [minor] Verses 19 and 27–31 cover the Kohathites generally, but verse 27 specifically mentions the Amramites. It may be clearer to focus the reference somewhat, but including context verses is not incorrect.; [minor] Amram's mother is not mentioned in the Bible, so zero is correct. However, it can be noted that rabbinic tradition sometimes speculates on this.; [minor] The Septuagint form is usually rendered as Ἀμράμ (Amram) in most manuscripts, not Ἀμβράμ (Ambram). The form with β occurs in some manuscripts, but the most common form should be mentioned.; [minor] Lev 18:12–13 deals with prohibitions against sexual relations with a father's sister and a mother's sister. Verse 12 alone covers the prohibition regarding a father's sister (which is relevant for Amram and Jochebed). Verse 13 concerns a mother's sister and is technically not directly relevant here, but including both provides context.

footnotes.text: The name Amram (Hebrew: עַמְרָם, 'Amram) likely means 'exalted people' or 'the high people', composed of עַם ('am, 'people') and רָם (ram, 'high/exalted'). This may reflect a hope for the future vindication of the people during a time of oppression in Egypt.

The marriage between Amram and Jochebed was a marriage between nephew and aunt (Exod 6:20). This type of marriage was later explicitly forbidden in the Mosaic Law (Lev 18:12). The fact that Amram's marriage took place before the law was given illustrates how family practices changed over time in line with revealed legislation. Rabbinic tradition discusses this relationship extensively.

In rabbinic literature (Talmud, Sotah 12a), Amram is portrayed as an important leader among the Israelites in Egypt. According to this tradition, he initially separated from Jochebed due to Pharaoh's death decree against Hebrew male infants, but was persuaded by his daughter Miriam to reunite with her, which led to Moses' birth.

Scholars debate whether the genealogy in Exod 6 represents direct father-son relationships or is a shortened lineage. If the stay in Egypt lasted 430 years (Exod 12:40), there may have been several generations between Kohath and Moses than what is listed. Amram's lifespan of 137 years could thus represent the lifespan of a clan leader rather than that of a direct biological father.

The Amramites are mentioned as one of the Levitical clans with special responsibility for the tabernacle and its holy objects, including the ark of the covenant, the table, the lampstand, the altars, and the curtain (Num 3:27-31). This clan held a prominent position among the Levites and played a key role in Israel's worship.

In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (Septuagint), Amram's name is usually rendered as Ἀμράμ (Amram). The name form also appears in various variants in other ancient translations and in the Dead Sea Scrolls, showing that this person was well known in the broader Jewish and early Christian tradition.

The Qumran text known as 'Amram's Visions' (4Q543-548) is an Aramaic text from the Dead Sea Scrolls that attributes a vision with apocalyptic content to Amram. The text is fragmentary but testifies that Amram held an important place in Jewish tradition beyond what is preserved in the canonical scriptures.
